value.overview: The Blue-and-white Swallow is a small, widespread swallow of Central and South America. Recognized by its glossy blue upperparts and clean white underparts, it is commonly seen flying over towns, farmland, grassland, water, and forest clearings. It catches insects in the air and readily uses buildings, bridges, banks, and natural cavities for nesting. Northern populations are mainly resident, while many birds from the southern part of the range migrate north after breeding.
value.classification: Pygochelidon cyanoleuca belongs to the swallow family Hirundinidae within the order Passeriformes. Several subspecies are recognized, including the larger, strongly migratory southern form P. c. patagonica.
value.identification: Adults are about 11–14 cm long, with glossy dark blue to blue-black upperparts and sharply contrasting white cheeks, throat, breast, and belly. The wings are pointed, and the short, slightly forked tail appears dark underneath. The bill, legs, and eyes are dark. Males and females look similar. Juveniles are duller, with brownish upperparts, buff-tinged underparts, and a less distinct tail fork. Flight is quick and fluttering, often interrupted by glides and brief periods perched on wires or exposed branches.
value.rangeHabitat: The species breeds from Nicaragua south through Costa Rica and much of South America to Tierra del Fuego. In Costa Rica it is a common resident mainly in the highlands, using towns, villages, farmland, pasture, forest clearings, lakeshores, and other open landscapes. Buildings, bridges, banks, and natural cavities provide nesting sites. Elsewhere it ranges from lowlands to about 4,000 meters in the Andes, although it is largely absent from extensive Amazonian forest and the driest deserts.
value.migrationStatus: Partially migratory. Northern and tropical populations are mostly resident or make local movements, while southern populations migrate north after breeding, sometimes reaching northern South America and Trinidad.
value.breeding: Blue-and-white Swallows nest in enclosed or sheltered sites, including holes in trees, earthen banks, rock crevices, rodent burrows, bridges, walls, roofs, and other structures. Both members of the pair build a shallow nest of dry grass or straw, often with a softer lining. Clutch size varies geographically, commonly ranging from two or three eggs in tropical areas to four, five, or occasionally six farther south. Both parents attend the nest, incubate the white eggs, and feed the young. Nestlings usually fledge after about three to four weeks.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of flying insects, including flies, beetles, wasps, winged ants, and termites. Birds capture prey in continuous aerial pursuit over open ground, water, treetops, roads, and buildings. They may gather in loose feeding groups where insects are concentrated, especially during termite or ant swarms. Foraging flight is agile and often low, although birds also feed high above the landscape. They regularly pause on wires, fences, bare branches, roofs, and other exposed perches.
value.behavior: This active, conspicuous swallow is usually seen alone, in pairs, or in small groups, with larger flocks forming outside the breeding season and during migration. It often associates with other swallows while feeding or resting. Birds frequently perch on utility wires and buildings between aerial feeding bouts. Pairs may remain closely associated and share nesting duties. The species adapts readily to settled areas and commonly nests near people. Its calls include buzzing, twittering, and chattering notes delivered in flight or from a perch.

conservation.status: Least Concern on the IUCN Red List. The species has an extensive range and remains common in many suitable habitats.
conservation.populationTrend: Decreasing globally, although the decline is not considered rapid enough to place the species in a threatened category.
conservation.threats: No major range-wide threat is known. Possible pressures include local loss of nesting cavities, disturbance or destruction of active nests, and reduced availability of flying insects associated with pesticide use and habitat degradation.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect active nests and retain safe nesting cavities in buildings, bridges, banks, and mature trees. Limit unnecessary insecticide use, maintain insect-rich open habitats and wetlands, and avoid disturbing colonies during the breeding season.
